clue.text: Elegant exterior to army compound

indicators.note: the first piece is placed on the outside of the second, wrapping round it

parts.note: posh means smart or elegant
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: A fancy outer casing around a military camp.
explanation.definitionFit: Potash is a potassium compound, used as fertiliser, so it is an example of a chemical compound.

clue.text: Mint gets senior pupil churning over inside

indicators.note: letters within the word turn over, changing their order in the middle while the ends stay

parts.note: a prefect is a senior pupil given authority in a British school

explanation.surface: A head boy or girl gets a stomach-churning feeling inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'churning over inside' swaps the R and E in the middle of PREFECT: the R moves one place along.
explanation.definitionFit: Mint condition means flawless, so as an adjective mint means perfect.

clue.text: That time for strangling good old aristocrat

indicators.note: something strangling has its grip round another's neck, so the second piece goes inside

parts.note: then means at that time

explanation.surface: Back then, a noble was throttled.
explanation.definitionFit: A thegn was a nobleman in Anglo-Saxon England, ranking above an ordinary freeman.

clue.text: Piece of music in street upset animal

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: an otter is an animal

explanation.surface: An animal in the street knocked over.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretto is a passage, especially in a fugue, where entries overlap, so it is a piece of music.

clue.text: Insects that might be said to make journeys in Wexford?

indicators.note: the word is to be heard spoken rather than read as written
Wexford is an Irish county, so the word is spoken in an Irish accent, where a T often sounds like TH

parts.note: trips are journeys, so to make them is to trip

explanation.surface: A question about insects that travel around County Wexford.
explanation.walkthrough: In a stereotyped Irish accent TRIPS comes out with a TH sound at the start; Wexford is a county in the south-east of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrips are tiny winged insects, pests of crops also called thunderflies.

clue.text: No land said to be a location of religious significance

indicators.note: the words are spoken, and what is heard gives the entry

parts.note: a place with no land at all is wholly sea

explanation.surface: Somewhere described as having no land at all turns out to be sacred.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy See is the jurisdiction of the Pope in Rome, a place of great religious importance.

clue.text: Like many a competitive golfer visible to all

definitions.meaning: playing ..., the British Open golf championship
out where everyone can see, not concealed

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both entered in the Open golf championship and exposed to general view.

clue.text: Bread taken when there's litre to be drunk

indicators.note: something drunk is taken in, so the letter goes inside the word

parts.note: stolen means taken without permission

explanation.surface: A loaf is pinched while a litre of drink goes down.
explanation.definitionFit: Stollen is a German fruit bread, eaten at Christmas.

clue.text: Bird may be a singer, but not one tenor

indicators.note: the named letter is left out of the word

parts.note: a singer may be described as a voice, as in a fine voice
the Roman numeral I stands for one

explanation.surface: A bird might be a songster, though not a single tenor among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be a singer' tempts you to look for a songbird, but the singer is a voice; 'but not' removes the one.
explanation.definitionFit: The avocet is a black-and-white wading bird with an upturned bill.

clue.text: Ignore volunteer working for agricultural improvement

indicators.note: the letters are put to work in a new order, as a machine's parts move when working

explanation.surface: Someone tells you to ignore the volunteer who is busy on a farming project.
explanation.definitionFit: The Green Revolution was the mid-twentieth-century surge in crop yields from new seeds and fertilisers, a landmark improvement in agriculture.

clue.text: One leaving square to be patrolled by black horse

indicators.note: being patrolled by something means having it go all round you, so the second piece sits inside the first

parts.note: jet is a deep glossy black

indicators.note: the named letter departs from the word

parts.note: nine is a square number, three times three
the Roman numeral I stands for one

explanation.surface: A lone figure leaves a town square guarded by a dark horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'square' here is a square number, not a town square; 'leaving' drops the one, and 'to be patrolled by' puts the rest inside black.
explanation.definitionFit: A jennet is a small Spanish riding horse, so it is a kind of horse.

clue.text: Singer with instrument entertaining 'undreds of people?

indicators.note: to entertain is to hold or take in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a cello is a stringed instrument
a host is a great many people; with the H dropped, as the apostrophe in 'undreds shows, it becomes OST

explanation.surface: A singer with a cello plays to a vast crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'undreds signals a dropped H, in the Cockney manner, so the HOST of people loses its H too.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvis Costello is a British singer-songwriter, so the surname names a singer.

clue.text: Keep an eye on Keats' formulation?

parts.note: read the other way, the letters of a word spelt anew with out as an anagram signal would give Keats, so the clue words describe the wordplay rather than giving it

explanation.surface: A question about how the poet Keats framed his words.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: read STAKE OUT as wordplay, with OUT as an anagram signal, and it says rearrange STAKE, which makes KEATS.
explanation.definitionFit: To stake out a place is to watch it covertly, keeping it under surveillance.

clue.text: Exhausted genius, before going to bed finally

parts.note: a knack or genius is a natural gift for something
ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: the final letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A brilliant mind is worn out before finally going to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Knackered is British slang for very tired.
explanation.definitionFit: Knackered is British slang for utterly worn out, the same as exhausted.

clue.text: Swell old lover subsequently criticised audibly

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: the word is to be heard spoken rather than read as written

parts.note: panned means harshly criticised, as a film by reviewers

explanation.surface: A former partner later got a slating, said to be heard swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subsequently' only puts the second piece after the first. PANNED said aloud sounds like PAND.
explanation.definitionFit: To expand is to grow larger, which is what something does when it swells.

clue.text: News feature gets cut, having gone over page

indicators.note: one piece goes over and round the other, so the second ends up inside the first

parts.note: a slash is a cut or gash

explanation.surface: A newspaper story is trimmed after running on to another page.
explanation.definitionFit: A splash is a prominent front-page newspaper story, so it is a feature of the news.

clue.text: Pretend agreement will cover non-professional

indicators.note: the first piece covers the second by going round it

parts.note: a pact is an agreement
lay means not belonging to a profession, as a layman

explanation.surface: A contract that will protect an amateur.
explanation.definitionFit: To play-act is to pretend or put on a show, behaving theatrically rather than sincerely.

clue.text: Surname of author coming at end of epigraph

definitions.text: Surname of author coming at end of epigraph

parts.words: Surname of author coming at end of epigraph
parts.note: an epigraph quotation is signed with its writer's name at the foot, and one much-quoted poet's surname often appears there

explanation.surface: A note on where a writer's name sits under a quotation.
explanation.walkthrough: George Herbert, the 17th-century religious poet, is often quoted in epigraphs; A. P. Herbert and Frank Herbert are other authors of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert is the surname of several authors, including the poet George Herbert, whose lines often head books.

clue.text: I love France, possibly for the drink there

indicators.note: the letters might possibly be arranged otherwise, so they are reordered

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone declares love for France and wonders what to drink there.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is French for black coffee, which is why 'there' refers back to France.
explanation.definitionFit: Cafe noir is black coffee, a drink that would be ordered in France.

clue.text: Firm with a bit of a hit makes money abroad

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm
a peck is a light quick blow, only a bit of a hit

explanation.surface: A company with a modest success earns cash overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: The copeck is a Russian coin, a hundredth of a rouble, so it is foreign money.

clue.text: Gathering storm

definitions.meaning: a strip of fabric gathered and sewn on as a frill
to storm off, moving with angry jerky gestures

explanation.definitionFit: A flounce is a gathered frill on a skirt, and to flounce is to storm out in a temper.

clue.text: Patient having no effect

definitions.meaning: a sick person, someone being cared for

explanation.definitionFit: Stressed on the first syllable it means a sick person; on the second it means not valid or void.

clue.text: Setting in theatre to support medic before operation

parts.note: to back someone is to support them
DR is the abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A theatre scene where a doctor gets ready for surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' tempts toward an operating theatre, which the medic and operation encourage, but here it is the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A backdrop is the painted cloth at the back of a stage, giving the scene's setting.

clue.text: Musical interval at 8 roughly

indicators.note: done roughly, the letters are handled loosely and come out in a different order

parts.note: 8 refers to the answer at 8 down, the wading bird

explanation.surface: A musical gap found at number eight, give or take.
explanation.walkthrough: The 8 is a cross-reference to the answer of 8 down, AVOCET, whose letters rearranged give the interval; 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The interval between a note and the next of the same name, spanning eight notes of the scale, named from Latin octo.

clue.text: Bear in Gleneagles demolishing hotel

indicators.note: a building being demolished is broken up, so the word's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone puts up with the knocking down of a hotel at the famous Scottish resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Gleneagles is a famous hotel and golf resort in Scotland, and the answer is a Scots word, hence 'in Gleneagles'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thole is a Scots and northern dialect verb meaning to endure or put up with.

clue.text: See sportswoman run on lamely, once injured

indicators.note: something injured is damaged and out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An athlete who was once hurt hobbles along.
explanation.walkthrough: Maureen Connolly, 'Little Mo', was an American tennis player who won the Grand Slam in 1953; her career ended after a riding injury.
explanation.definitionFit: Maureen Connolly was a champion tennis player, so she is an example of a sportswoman.

clue.text: Fox didn't go hungry until now

parts.note: tod is an old and dialect word for a fox
someone who did not go hungry ate

explanation.surface: A fox found food at last.
explanation.definitionFit: To date means up to the present moment, the same as so far or until now.

clue.text: Nymph seen as Newcastle's answer to Beryl?

parts.note: NE is the postcode area for Newcastle upon Tyne
Beryl Reid was a British comic actress, so Reid is the surname that answers to the name Beryl

explanation.surface: A question about whether Newcastle has its own version of a woman named Beryl.
explanation.walkthrough: Beryl Reid was a British comedy actress; beryl the gemstone is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nereid is a sea nymph of Greek myth, a daughter of Nereus.
